newsitem.title: UK: UK insurance brokers defend self regulation.
newsitem.headline: UK insurance brokers defend self regulation.

text.p: Independent insurance intermediaries in the UK have called for regulation of their sector to remain in their own hands and not be handed over to a government body.

Ian Ritchie, chairman of the Insurance Brokers Registration Council, told an insurance industry conference on Friday: "I would be more than a little concerned for the future of independent advice if regulation of the entire insurance market came under the auspices of one regulator or one government department."
Ritchie said that voluntary regulation of insurance brokers had spread professionalism without government pressure or other outside interests.

"We have been willing to grasp the nettle and respond to the constant gibe of the early 1970s that insurance brokers should put their house in order. Anyone seeking to obstruct our efforts will need to consider their motives and be judged on the extent of their self interest," he said.

Ritchie accepted that there had been a lack of public confidence and a disenchantment with the market's performance. He said this was largely due to complacent management, over-capacity in the market and a lack of government support.
"We have had a government which believes that competition was all and competitiveness has been translated as meaning cheap," he said.
But he told delegates at the Chartered Insurance Institute conference in Newcastle that he was unhappy with the current situation.
"If the insurance market were prepared to accept development of a regulated intermediary sector there would be benefits to each and every sector involved with insurance," said Ritchie.
"I do not believe there is any evidence that the Financial Services Act's form of regulation is cost effective or a positive force in the development of the investment market," he added.

"The current structure of the Securities Investment Board and the Personal Investment Authority does not produce a constructive facility to develop the business because of its negative and confrontational format," he said.
